claims.source: Loss of NR2E3 leads to enhanced S-cone syndrome, an autosomal recessive human retinal disease (Haider et al., 2000) that is recapitulated in retinal degeneration 7 (rd7) mice (Haider et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Haider et al., 2000 and 2001.

claims.claim: rd7 rods retain expression of rod-specific genes but also de-repress a subset of cone-specific genes.
claims.source: rd7 rods show a partial conversion of photoreceptor identity because they retain expression of rod-specific genes but also de-repress a subset of cone-specific genes (Chen et al., 2005; Corbo and Cepko, 2005; Peng et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2005; Corbo and Cepko, 2005; Peng et al., 2005.

claims.claim: Rods make up 70–80% of all mouse retinal cells.
claims.source: Because rods make up 70–80% of all mouse retinal cells and outnumber cones by 35:1 (Jeon et al., 1998), whole retina studies can approximate features of rods but mask differences between rods and cones that contribute to their unique identities.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jeon et al., 1998.

claims.claim: Rods outnumber cones by 35:1 in mouse retina.
claims.source: Because rods make up 70–80% of all mouse retinal cells and outnumber cones by 35:1 (Jeon et al., 1998), whole retina studies can approximate features of rods but mask differences between rods and cones that contribute to their unique identities.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jeon et al., 1998.

claims.claim: There is a high positive correlation between accessible chromatin and local regions of low DNA methylation in various cell types.
claims.source: Of special interest is the high positive correlation between accessible chromatin and local regions of low DNA methylation that has been observed in various cell types (Stadler et al., 2011; Hon et al., 2013; Ziller et al., 2013; Mo et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: TF binding can result in local regions of low DNA methylation.
claims.source: TF binding can result in local regions of low DNA methylation, leading to strong overlaps between regions identified as DNA hypo-methylated and as accessible chromatin.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: The rod nucleus is approximately 5 μm in size.
claims.source: Also of interest is the small size of the rod nucleus (~5 μm; Solovei et al., 2009) and its highly condensed chromatin (Kizilyaprak et al., 2010), which may potentially impact how chromatin accessibility correlates with DNA methylation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Solovei et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Rod nuclei have highly condensed chromatin.
claims.source: Also of interest is the small size of the rod nucleus (~5 μm; Solovei et al., 2009) and its highly condensed chromatin (Kizilyaprak et al., 2010), which may potentially impact how chromatin accessibility correlates with DNA methylation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kizilyaprak et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Rods are the only known cell type in mice with nuclei that have heterochromatin centers surrounded by peripheral euchromatin.
claims.source: In addition, rods are the only known cell type in mice with nuclei that have heterochromatin centers surrounded by peripheral euchromatin (Carter-Dawson and LaVail, 1979).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Carter-Dawson and LaVail, 1979.

claims.claim: The inverted chromatin organization in rods is thought to facilitate nocturnal vision.
claims.source: This inverted organization is thought to facilitate nocturnal vision (Solovei et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Solovei et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Cone nuclei are larger than rod nuclei and exhibit the conventional arrangement of central euchromatin and peripheral heterochromatin.
claims.source: By contrast, cone nuclei are larger and exhibit the conventional arrangement of central euchromatin and peripheral heterochromatin.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a comparison to rod nuclei based on established knowledge.

claims.claim: Most rod-specific regions of low DNA methylation are not located in accessible chromatin in adult rods.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, most rod-specific regions of low DNA methylation are not located in accessible chromatin in adult rods.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis.

claims.claim: Rod-specific hypo-methylated regions that are not in accessible chromatin are potential active regulatory sites in fetal neural tissue.
claims.source: Instead, our evidence suggests that these regions are potential active regulatory sites in fetal neural tissue and, despite loss of active chromatin marks, remain hypo-methylated in adult rods due to the barrier to cytosine methyltransferases posed by chromatin condensation.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the study's data comparing adult and fetal samples.

claims.claim: Hypo-methylated regions in adult rods remain unmethylated due to the barrier to cytosine methyltransferases posed by chromatin condensation.
claims.source: Instead, our evidence suggests that these regions are potential active regulatory sites in fetal neural tissue and, despite loss of active chromatin marks, remain hypo-methylated in adult rods due to the barrier to cytosine methyltransferases posed by chromatin condensation.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the study's findings.

claims.claim: NR2E3 function is necessary for rods to gain their complete ensemble of epigenomic features.
claims.source: Integrated analysis of rd7 rods, together with normal rods and cones, shows that NR2E3 function is necessary for rods to gain their complete ensemble of epigenomic features.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the integrated analysis of rd7 rods compared to normal rods and cones.

claims.claim: 16617 rod and 15888 cone discrete unmethylated regions (UMRs) were identified with median mCG = 6%.
claims.source: Using previously defined criteria (Stadler et al., 2011; Burger et al., 2013), we identified two types of regions that are depleted for DNA methylation: (1) 16617 rod and 15888 cone discrete (<5 kb) un-methylated regions (UMRs; median mCG = 6%), which tend to be at promoters, and (2) 85992 rod and 65791 cone low-methylated regions (LMRs; median mCG = 24%), which are likely associated with distal regulatory regions (Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the MethylC-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: 85992 rod and 65791 cone low-methylated regions (LMRs) were identified with median mCG = 24%.
claims.source: Using previously defined criteria (Stadler et al., 2011; Burger et al., 2013), we identified two types of regions that are depleted for DNA methylation: (1) 16617 rod and 15888 cone discrete (<5 kb) un-methylated regions (UMRs; median mCG = 6%), which tend to be at promoters, and (2) 85992 rod and 65791 cone low-methylated regions (LMRs; median mCG = 24%), which are likely associated with distal regulatory regions (Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the MethylC-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: 55366 regions in rods and 75650 regions in cones with increased ATAC-seq densities mark accessible chromatin.
claims.source: We identified a set of 55366 regions in rods and 75650 regions in cones with increased ATAC-seq densities that mark accessible chromatin (Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the ATAC-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: In both rods and cones, ATAC-seq peaks exhibit low levels of DNA methylation.
claims.source: In both rods and cones, ATAC-seq peaks exhibit low levels of DNA methylation (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Hypo-methylated regions have elevated ATAC-seq signals on average.
claims.source: On average, hypo-methylated regions also have elevated ATAC-seq signals (Figure 1C), and UMRs show strong overlap with ATAC-seq peaks (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: UMRs show strong overlap with ATAC-seq peaks.
claims.source: On average, hypo-methylated regions also have elevated ATAC-seq signals (Figure 1C), and UMRs show strong overlap with ATAC-seq peaks (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: 38% of cone LMRs overlap with ATAC-seq peaks.
claims.source: 38% (24830) of cone LMRs overlap with ATAC-seq peaks, a percentage close to previous reports in embryonic stem cells and cortical neurons (Xie et al., 2013; Mo et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis comparing LMRs and ATAC-seq peaks.

claims.claim: Only 19% of rod LMRs overlap with ATAC-seq peaks.
claims.source: Yet, only 19% (15984) of rod LMRs overlap with ATAC-seq peaks.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis comparing LMRs and ATAC-seq peaks.

claims.claim: 31% of rod LMRs show no sign of chromatin accessibility (<0.1 ATAC-seq FPKM).
claims.source: In fact, 31% of rod LMRs show no sign of chromatin accessibility (<0.1 ATAC-seq FPKM), whereas this fraction is only 7% for cones.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis.

claims.claim: Only 7% of cone LMRs show no sign of chromatin accessibility (<0.1 ATAC-seq FPKM).
claims.source: In fact, 31% of rod LMRs show no sign of chromatin accessibility (<0.1 ATAC-seq FPKM), whereas this fraction is only 7% for cones.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis.

claims.claim: Rods harbor a substantial compartment of demethylated, but inaccessible, DNA that is largely absent in cones.
claims.source: This analysis shows that rods harbor a substantial compartment of demethylated, but inaccessible, DNA that is largely absent in cones.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative analysis of rods and cones.

claims.claim: 49% of cone LMRs overlap Nrl KO ATAC-seq peaks.
claims.source: Similar to our results using purified nuclei, a greater fraction of cone LMRs overlap Nrl KO ATAC-seq peaks (49%; 31952) compared to rod LMRs that overlap WT ATAC-seq peaks (26%; 22590) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis using whole retina samples.

claims.claim: 26% of rod LMRs overlap WT ATAC-seq peaks.
claims.source: Similar to our results using purified nuclei, a greater fraction of cone LMRs overlap Nrl KO ATAC-seq peaks (49%; 31952) compared to rod LMRs that overlap WT ATAC-seq peaks (26%; 22590) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis using whole retina samples.

claims.claim: A subset of active enhancers in embryonic tissue have low levels of DNA methylation in adult tissues in the absence of ongoing enhancer activity.
claims.source: A previous study demonstrated that a subset of active enhancers in embryonic tissue have low levels of DNA methylation in adult tissues in the absence of ongoing enhancer activity (Hon et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hon et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Vestigial enhancers are hypo-methylated regions that are not enriched for active histone marks and DNaseI hypersensitivity in adult cells.
claims.source: Referred to as vestigial enhancers, these hypo-methylated regions are not enriched for active histone marks and DNaseI hypersensitivity in adult cells.
claims.evidence: This is a definition based on previous literature.

claims.claim: Rod LMRs have a bimodal distribution of <100 bp ATAC-seq signals.
claims.source: When we examine the densities of sub-nucleosomal-length ATAC-seq reads, a subset of reads that may better capture sites of TF binding (He et al., 2014), we observe a bimodal distribution of rod ATAC-seq signals at LMRs (Figure 1E), with the lower peak at nearly zero signal.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: The distribution of rod ATAC-seq signals at LMRs is significantly different from that of cone ATAC-seq signals at LMRs (bootstrap Kolmogorov-Smirnov p<2.2 x 10–16).
claims.source: This distribution is significantly different than that of cone ATAC-seq signals at LMRs (bootstrap Kolmogorov-Smirnov p<2.2 x 10–16) and potentially reflects a greater number of vestigial enhancers in rod, compared to cone, LMRs.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claims.claim: There are more DMRs with lower methylation levels in rods than in cones (10784 rod hypo-DMRs versus 6693 cone hypo-DMRs).
claims.source: We find a greater number of DMRs that have lower methylation levels (hypo-DMRs) in rods than in cones (10784 rod hypo-DMRs versus 6693 cone hypo-DMRs).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the DMR analysis.

claims.claim: DNA methylation levels at DMRs around gene transcription start sites show a strong negative correlation with gene expression, with a trough Pearson correlation of -0.8 4 kb downstream of the TSS.
claims.source: As expected from previous studies (Schultz et al., 2015), DNA methylation levels at DMRs around gene transcription start sites (TSSs) show a strong negative correlation with gene expression, with a trough Pearson correlation of -0.8 4 kb downstream of the TSS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and is consistent with previous studies.

claims.claim: Only 3% of rod hypo-DMRs overlap rod ATAC-seq peaks.
claims.source: Similar to our results using LMRs, we find that rod hypo-DMRs are especially discordant with accessible chromatin: only 307 (3%) of rod hypo-DMRs overlap rod ATAC-seq peaks, compared with 1475 (22%) of cone hypo-DMRs that overlap cone ATAC-seq peaks (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis.

claims.claim: 22% of cone hypo-DMRs overlap cone ATAC-seq peaks.
claims.source: Similar to our results using LMRs, we find that rod hypo-DMRs are especially discordant with accessible chromatin: only 307 (3%) of rod hypo-DMRs overlap rod ATAC-seq peaks, compared with 1475 (22%) of cone hypo-DMRs that overlap cone ATAC-seq peaks (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis.

claims.claim: The large majority of rod hypo-DMRs are depleted for ATAC-seq signal.
claims.source: In rods the large majority of hypo-DMRs are depleted for ATAC-seq signal (Figures 2C–D), active histone modifications H3K4me1 and H3K27ac (Figure 2E), and retinal photoreceptor TF binding (Figure 2F), and they are located distally from promoters (Figure 2G; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 2C-D.

claims.claim: The large majority of rod hypo-DMRs are depleted for active histone modifications H3K4me1 and H3K27ac.
claims.source: In rods the large majority of hypo-DMRs are depleted for ATAC-seq signal (Figures 2C–D), active histone modifications H3K4me1 and H3K27ac (Figure 2E), and retinal photoreceptor TF binding (Figure 2F), and they are located distally from promoters (Figure 2G; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: The large majority of rod hypo-DMRs are depleted for retinal photoreceptor TF binding.
claims.source: In rods the large majority of hypo-DMRs are depleted for ATAC-seq signal (Figures 2C–D), active histone modifications H3K4me1 and H3K27ac (Figure 2E), and retinal photoreceptor TF binding (Figure 2F), and they are located distally from promoters (Figure 2G; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: Rod hypo-DMRs are located distally from promoters.
claims.source: In rods the large majority of hypo-DMRs are depleted for ATAC-seq signal (Figures 2C–D), active histone modifications H3K4me1 and H3K27ac (Figure 2E), and retinal photoreceptor TF binding (Figure 2F), and they are located distally from promoters (Figure 2G; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Most rod hypo-DMRs have low levels of DNA methylation in fetal cortex.
claims.source: Supporting the idea that rod hypo-DMRs may be enriched for enhancers that function earlier in neural development, most rod hypo-DMRs have low levels of DNA methylation in fetal cortex (Figure 2C,H) and are enriched for active histone modifications in fetal brain (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 2C and 2H.

claims.claim: Most rod hypo-DMRs are enriched for active histone modifications in fetal brain.
claims.source: Supporting the idea that rod hypo-DMRs may be enriched for enhancers that function earlier in neural development, most rod hypo-DMRs have low levels of DNA methylation in fetal cortex (Figure 2C,H) and are enriched for active histone modifications in fetal brain (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: Disruption of NR2E3 in rd7 rods preserves the inverted chromatin arrangement but reduces chromatin condensation.
claims.source: To address this question, we took advantage of the observation that disruption of NR2E3 in rd7 rods preserves the inverted chromatin arrangement, but reduces chromatin condensation (Corbo and Cepko, 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Corbo and Cepko, 2005.

claims.claim: rd7 rods are hypo-methylated at rod hypo-DMRs but show higher methylation levels than WT rods.
claims.source: We find that whereas rd7 rods are also hypo-methylated at rod hypo-DMRs, including those that may encompass vestigial enhancers, they show higher methylation levels than WT rods (Figure 2C,H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 2C and 2H.

claims.claim: Chromatin condensation plays a role in limiting the methylation of vestigial enhancers.
claims.source: Taken together, these data are consistent with a role for chromatin condensation in limiting the methylation of vestigial enhancers.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the comparative data from WT and rd7 rods.

claims.claim: 22520 ATAC-seq peaks show >2-fold increased accessibility in Nrl KO retina.
claims.source: In comparing WT and Nrl KO retinas, 22520 ATAC-seq peaks show >2-fold increased accessibility in Nrl KO retina, but only about a third as many (7916 peaks) have greater accessibility in WT retina (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the differential ATAC-seq analysis.

claims.claim: 7916 ATAC-seq peaks show >2-fold increased accessibility in WT retina.
claims.source: In comparing WT and Nrl KO retinas, 22520 ATAC-seq peaks show >2-fold increased accessibility in Nrl KO retina, but only about a third as many (7916 peaks) have greater accessibility in WT retina (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the differential ATAC-seq analysis.

claims.claim: WT-enriched regions of accessible chromatin cluster near the promoters of rod-specific genes.
claims.source: WT-enriched regions of accessible chromatin cluster near the promoters of rod-specific genes (Supplementary file 5) and have high levels of H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and H3K4me3 (Figure 3B–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 3B-D and Supplementary file 5.

claims.claim: WT-enriched accessible chromatin regions have high levels of H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and H3K4me3.
claims.source: WT-enriched regions of accessible chromatin cluster near the promoters of rod-specific genes (Supplementary file 5) and have high levels of H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and H3K4me3 (Figure 3B–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 3B-D.

claims.claim: Nrl KO-enriched accessible chromatin cluster near promoters of cone-specific genes.
claims.source: In contrast, Nrl KO-enriched accessible chromatin cluster near promoters of cone-specific genes (Figure 3B,C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claims.claim: A higher percentage of NRL binding sites overlap WT-enriched ATAC-seq peaks rather than Nrl KO-enriched peaks.
claims.source: A higher percentage of binding sites for NRL and CRX in WT retina overlap WT-enriched, rather than Nrl KO-enriched, peaks (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: A higher percentage of CRX binding sites in WT retina overlap WT-enriched ATAC-seq peaks rather than Nrl KO-enriched peaks.
claims.source: A higher percentage of binding sites for NRL and CRX in WT retina overlap WT-enriched, rather than Nrl KO-enriched, peaks (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: CRX binding sites in Nrl KO retina show higher overlap with Nrl KO-enriched peaks.
claims.source: However, CRX binding sites in Nrl KO retina show higher overlap with Nrl KO-enriched peaks.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the analysis of CRX ChIP-seq data in Nrl KO retina.

claims.claim: One previously identified enhancer near Nr2e3 induced reporter activity in WT but not in Nrl KO retinas.
claims.source: Within the sensitivity limits of the assay, one previously identified enhancer near Nr2e3 (Hsiau et al., 2007) induced reporter activity in WT but not in Nrl KO retinas (Figure 4, top), and four out of five regions near cone-specific genes induced reporter activity in Nrl KO but not in WT retinas (Figure 4, bottom; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Four out of five regions near cone-specific genes induced reporter activity in Nrl KO but not in WT retinas.
claims.source: Within the sensitivity limits of the assay, one previously identified enhancer near Nr2e3 (Hsiau et al., 2007) induced reporter activity in WT but not in Nrl KO retinas (Figure 4, top), and four out of five regions near cone-specific genes induced reporter activity in Nrl KO but not in WT retinas (Figure 4, bottom; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The majority (5/6) of regions that had detectable reporter expression showed cell type-specificity.
claims.source: Although the electroporation experiments tested only a limited number of regions, the majority (5/6) of regions that had detectable reporter expression showed cell type-specificity.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the electroporation experiment results.

claims.claim: A motif matching the canonical CRX motif is enriched in all three peak sets (WT-specific, Nrl KO-specific, and shared) relative to random sequences.
claims.source: Consistent with CRX binding data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), a motif matching the canonical CRX motif (p<1 x 10–10; Gupta et al., 2007) is enriched in all three peak sets (WT-specific, Nrl KO-specific, and shared) relative to random sequences (Figure 5A, left) and is the top motif for both Nrl KO retina and shared peaks.
claims.evidence: This is supported by motif analysis data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: A motif matching CTCF shows the second strongest enrichment in shared peaks against random sequences.
claims.source: A motif matching CTCF (p<1 x 10–5) shows the second strongest enrichment in shared peaks against random sequences (Figure 5A, middle).
claims.evidence: This is supported by motif analysis data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: 87% of ATAC-seq peaks with the strongest (top 20%) CTCF binding sites show DNaseI hypersensitivity in >30% of mouse tissues surveyed by ENCODE.
claims.source: Shared peaks with the strongest CTCF binding sites appear to be located in accessible chromatin in a broad range of cell types: 87% of ATAC-seq peaks with the strongest (top 20%) CTCF binding sites show DNaseI hypersensitivity in >30% of mouse tissues surveyed by ENCODE (Stamatoyannopoulos et al., 2012), compared to only 35% of peaks in the remainder (bottom 80%) that lack strong CTCF binding sites.
claims.evidence: This is a result from comparing CTCF binding sites with ENCODE DNaseI hypersensitivity data.

claims.claim: Only 35% of ATAC-seq peaks in the bottom 80% that lack strong CTCF binding sites show DNaseI hypersensitivity in >30% of mouse tissues surveyed by ENCODE.
claims.source: Shared peaks with the strongest CTCF binding sites appear to be located in accessible chromatin in a broad range of cell types: 87% of ATAC-seq peaks with the strongest (top 20%) CTCF binding sites show DNaseI hypersensitivity in >30% of mouse tissues surveyed by ENCODE (Stamatoyannopoulos et al., 2012), compared to only 35% of peaks in the remainder (bottom 80%) that lack strong CTCF binding sites.
claims.evidence: This is a result from comparing CTCF binding sites with ENCODE DNaseI hypersensitivity data.

claims.claim: Gkm-SVM can distinguish Nrl KO-specific regions from random regions based on regulatory sequences with auROC = 0.91.
claims.source: Although the WT-specific set was too small for the gkm-SVM analysis, the Nrl KO-specific (auROC = 0.91) and shared (auROC = 0.86) regions can be distinguished from random regions based on regulatory sequences contained within the peaks (Figure 5B,C).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the gkm-SVM analysis shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claims.claim: Gkm-SVM can distinguish shared regions from random regions based on regulatory sequences with auROC = 0.86.
claims.source: Although the WT-specific set was too small for the gkm-SVM analysis, the Nrl KO-specific (auROC = 0.91) and shared (auROC = 0.86) regions can be distinguished from random regions based on regulatory sequences contained within the peaks (Figure 5B,C).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the gkm-SVM analysis shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claims.claim: Gkm-SVM trained on WT retina ATAC-seq could predict retinal enhancer activity as assessed by a massively parallel reporter assay.
claims.source: Further supporting the ability of our gkm-SVM model to predict enhancer activity, we find that a gkm-SVM trained on WT retina ATAC-seq could predict retinal enhancer activity as assessed by a massively parallel reporter assay (Shen et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of data from Shen et al., 2016.

claims.claim: The Pearson correlation between the gkm-SVM WT retina ATAC-seq score and the average retinal CRE expression level is 0.427 (p<10–320).
claims.source: Among the 12858 constructs with RNA detected in at least one replicate, the Pearson correlation between the gkm-SVM WT retina ATAC-seq score and the average retinal CRE expression level is 0.427 (p<10–320).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis of the massively parallel reporter assay data.

claims.claim: Candidate CREs that score in the top 10% of gkm-SVM scores are 4-fold enriched for high-level expression.
claims.source: Relative to all candidate CREs, those that score in the top 10% of gkm-SVM scores are 4-fold enriched for high-level expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Pearson correlations of ATAC-seq signal between rd7 and WT retina is r = 0.91.
claims.source: Pearson correlations of ATAC-seq signal between rd7 and WT retina (r = 0.91; Figure 6A) and between rd7 and Nrl KO retina (r = 0.88; Figure 6B) are both higher than the correlation between WT and Nrl KO retina (r = 0.78; Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the ATAC-seq data analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Pearson correlations of ATAC-seq signal between rd7 and Nrl KO retina is r = 0.88.
claims.source: Pearson correlations of ATAC-seq signal between rd7 and WT retina (r = 0.91; Figure 6A) and between rd7 and Nrl KO retina (r = 0.88; Figure 6B) are both higher than the correlation between WT and Nrl KO retina (r = 0.78; Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the ATAC-seq data analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The rd7 rod chromatin shows a hybrid rod/cone phenotype.
claims.source: These correlations indicate that the rd7 rod chromatin shows a hybrid rod/cone phenotype, recapitulating previous observations from gene expression studies (Chen et al., 2005; Corbo and Cepko, 2005; Peng et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the correlation data and is consistent with previous studies.

claims.claim: 44 ATAC-seq peaks within 10 kb of rod-specific genes show greater than two-fold higher signal in WT retina compared to rd7 retina.
claims.source: Notably, 44 ATAC-seq peaks within 10 kb of rod-specific genes show greater than two-fold higher signal in WT retina compared to rd7 retina, whereas only one peak displays the opposite pattern.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the differential ATAC-seq analysis.

claims.claim: Peaks near cone genes that are normally repressed in rods by NR2E3 show higher chromatin accessibility in rd7 retina compared to WT retina.
claims.source: Reciprocally, peaks near cone genes that are normally repressed in rods by NR2E3 (e.g., Gnat2, Pde6c, Pde6h, Gnb3) show higher chromatin accessibility in rd7 retina compared to WT retina.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the ATAC-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: Very few regions show differences in DNA methylation between rd7 rods and WT rods: 287 regions are hypo-DMRs in rd7 rods and 1385 regions are hypo-DMRs in WT rods.
claims.source: With respect to their DNA methylation, very few regions show differences between rd7 rods and WT rods: 287 regions are hypo-DMRs in rd7 rods and 1385 regions are hypo-DMRs in WT rods.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the DMR analysis.

claims.claim: A comparison of rd7 rod versus cone methylomes reveals 1981 regions that are hypo-DMRs in rd7 rods and 4929 regions that are hypo-DMRs in cones.
claims.source: A comparison of rd7 rod versus cone methylomes reveals more differences: 1981 regions are hypo-DMRs in rd7 rods and 4929 regions are hypo-DMRs in cones.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the DMR analysis.

claims.claim: Intragenic and promoter levels of DNA methylation are lower in rods at rod-specific genes and in cones at cone-specific genes.
claims.source: Consistent with previous studies in the retina at targeted genes (Merbs et al., 2012) or using enrichment-based methylation assays (Oliver et al., 2013), intragenic and promoter levels of DNA methylation are lower in rods at rod-specific genes and in cones at cone-specific genes (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C and is consistent with previous studies.

claims.claim: At rod-specific genes, rd7 rod methylation levels generally resemble those seen in WT rods or lie midway between WT rods and cones.
claims.source: At rod-specific genes (e.g., Nrl, Esrrb, Cnga1), rd7 rod methylation levels generally resemble those seen in WT rods or lie midway between WT rods and cones (Figure 6C,D; Figure 6—figure supplement 1–2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 6C, 6D, and Figure 6—figure supplements 1-2.

results.result: The study identified unmethylated regions (UMRs) and low-methylated regions (LMRs) in rods and cones, and found that ATAC-seq peaks exhibit low DNA methylation while hypo-methylated regions show elevated ATAC-seq signals on average, with UMRs showing strong overlap with ATAC-seq peaks.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C27 provide quantitative data from MethylC-seq and ATAC-seq analyses showing the identification of specific numbers of UMRs and LMRs, and demonstrate the expected correlation between DNA methylation and chromatin accessibility. The data are internally consistent and supported by figures.

results.result: Rods show a substantially lower overlap between LMRs and ATAC-seq peaks (19%) compared to cones (38%), with 31% of rod LMRs showing no chromatin accessibility versus only 7% for cones, indicating that rods harbor a substantial compartment of demethylated but inaccessible DNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C32 present quantitative comparisons between rods and cones that are internally consistent and represent a major finding. The data are replicated using whole retina samples (C33-C34), strengthening the conclusion. This is a key discovery of the manuscript.

results.result: Rod LMRs exhibit a bimodal distribution of sub-nucleosomal ATAC-seq signals that is significantly different from cone LMRs (p<2.2×10⁻¹⁶), potentially reflecting a greater number of vestigial enhancers in rods.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C38 provide statistical evidence for a distinct distribution pattern in rods. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test is appropriate for comparing distributions, and the extremely low p-value supports the significance of the difference. The interpretation regarding vestigial enhancers is reasonable but speculative.

results.result: Differential methylation analysis identified more rod hypo-DMRs (10,784) than cone hypo-DMRs (6,693), with rod hypo-DMRs showing strong negative correlation with gene expression and being depleted for ATAC-seq signal, active histone modifications, and TF binding, and located distally from promoters.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C46 present a comprehensive characterization of DMRs with quantitative data and correlation analyses. The negative correlation between methylation and gene expression (r=-0.8) is consistent with established biology. The depletion patterns are well-documented in the figures.

results.result: Rod hypo-DMRs show low DNA methylation in fetal cortex and enrichment for active histone modifications in fetal brain, and rd7 rods show higher methylation at these regions than WT rods, supporting a role for chromatin condensation in limiting methylation of vestigial enhancers.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C48 and C50-C51 provide evidence linking rod hypo-DMRs to developmental enhancers and support the chromatin condensation hypothesis. The rd7 data provide a natural experiment testing this hypothesis. However, the mechanism remains correlative rather than causally demonstrated.

results.result: Comparison of WT and Nrl KO retinas identified 22,520 Nrl KO-enriched and 7,916 WT-enriched ATAC-seq peaks, with WT-enriched peaks clustering near rod-specific gene promoters with high active histone marks, while Nrl KO-enriched peaks cluster near cone-specific genes, and TF binding patterns match these distributions.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C59 provide comprehensive characterization of cell type-specific accessible chromatin with quantitative data, histone modification profiles, and TF binding validation. The data are internally consistent and well-supported by multiple lines of evidence including ChIP-seq.

results.result: In vivo electroporation experiments showed that one enhancer near Nr2e3 was active in WT but not Nrl KO retinas, while four out of five regions near cone genes were active in Nrl KO but not WT retinas, with 5/6 regions showing cell type-specificity.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C62 provide experimental validation of predicted regulatory elements. While the sample size is limited (acknowledged by authors), the majority of tested regions showed the expected cell type-specificity, supporting the predictive value of the epigenomic data.

results.result: Motif analysis identified CRX motif enrichment in all peak sets, CTCF motif enrichment in shared peaks, with 87% of peaks with strong CTCF binding showing DNaseI hypersensitivity in >30% of ENCODE tissues versus 35% for peaks lacking strong CTCF sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C66 provide motif analysis with statistical significance and validation against ENCODE data. The CRX enrichment is consistent with known biology, and the CTCF analysis provides insight into shared versus cell-specific regulatory elements.

results.result: Gkm-SVM analysis distinguished Nrl KO-specific (auROC=0.91) and shared (auROC=0.86) regions from random sequences, and predicted retinal enhancer activity in a massively parallel reporter assay with Pearson correlation of 0.427 (p<10⁻³²⁰), with top 10% scoring regions showing 4-fold enrichment for high-level expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C71 demonstrate strong predictive performance of the sequence-based model with appropriate validation using independent data. The auROC values indicate good discrimination, and the correlation with reporter assay data provides functional validation.

results.result: rd7 retina shows intermediate ATAC-seq patterns with correlations to WT (r=0.91) and Nrl KO (r=0.88) both higher than WT-Nrl KO correlation (r=0.78), with 44 peaks near rod genes showing higher signal in WT and peaks near NR2E3-repressed cone genes showing higher signal in rd7.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C76 demonstrate that rd7 rods have a hybrid epigenomic phenotype using correlation analysis and differential peak analysis. The data are consistent with previous gene expression studies and provide epigenomic validation of the partial cell fate conversion.

results.result: DNA methylation analysis of rd7 rods showed few differences from WT rods (287 rd7 hypo-DMRs, 1,385 WT hypo-DMRs) but more differences from cones (1,981 rd7 hypo-DMRs, 4,929 cone hypo-DMRs), with methylation patterns at photoreceptor-specific genes generally intermediate between WT rods and cones, except for Aqp1.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C82 provide quantitative DMR analysis and gene-specific examples showing the hybrid methylation state of rd7 rods. The data are consistent with the ATAC-seq findings and supported by figures. The Aqp1 exception is interesting but not explained.

results.result: DNA methylation valley (DMV) analysis identified 782 WT rod, 635 rd7 rod, and 816 cone DMVs (≥5 kb), with 89-90% within 2.5 kb of TSS and 93-94% overlapping gene bodies, enriched for DNA-binding factors, showing cell type-specific methylation patterns at developmental TF genes including Onecut1.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C87, C89-C90 provide comprehensive DMV characterization with quantitative data and GO enrichment analysis. The enrichment for TF genes is consistent with previous studies. The cell type-specific patterns at developmental genes like Onecut1 provide biological insight.

results.result: Rods and cones have similar mCG levels to cortical neurons but 29- and 7-fold lower mCH levels respectively, with WT rods showing 0.11-0.13% mCH, cones 0.42-0.45%, and rd7 rods intermediate at 0.21-0.25%, suggesting post-mitotic mCH accumulation in photoreceptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C97 provide quantitative methylation data comparing photoreceptors to neurons. The fold-change calculations are clear, and the intermediate rd7 levels support the inference about post-mitotic accumulation, though this remains correlative rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: Hierarchical clustering showed retinal photoreceptors cluster separately from cortical neurons, with cortical neurons showing greater inter-subtype distance than rod-cone distance, and fetal cortex clustering closer to mature photoreceptors than to mature cortical neurons, with twice as many retinal-specific (63,384) versus cortical-specific (31,483) hypo-DMRs.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C102 provide clustering analysis and DMR quantification comparing retinal and cortical samples. The interpretation that cortical neurons acquire more extensive cell type-specific modifications is reasonable but somewhat speculative. The data support the clustering patterns described.

results.result: The authors propose that increased chromatin condensation in rods poses a barrier to DNA methyltransferases, supported by rd7 rods having slightly increased nuclear size and lower chromatin condensation showing higher methylation at vestigial enhancers, and by previous observations of low mCH in dense heterochromatin regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C106 present a mechanistic hypothesis that is plausible and supported by correlative evidence from rd7 rods and literature. However, the mechanism is not directly tested - no experiments manipulate chromatin condensation or methyltransferase access independently. The hypothesis remains speculative despite supporting correlations.

results.result: The finding that rods show fewer accessible chromatin regions than cones suggests rods represent a more developmentally restricted cell type at the epigenomic level, consistent with models proposing NRL and NR2E3 direct precursors away from the default S-cone fate.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C110 provide an interpretation of the ATAC-seq data in the context of developmental models. The interpretation is reasonable and consistent with cited literature, though it represents a conceptual framework rather than direct experimental evidence of developmental restriction.

results.result: Integrated analysis shows rd7 rods fail to attain WT rod levels of chromatin accessibility and DNA hypo-methylation at rod-specific regions while exhibiting increased accessibility and hypo-methylation at cone-specific regions and intermediate patterns at developmental TF gene DMVs, demonstrating NR2E3 is necessary for rods to gain their complete epigenomic features.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C113, C21, C91-C92 synthesize multiple lines of evidence showing rd7 rods have incomplete rod and partial cone epigenomic features. The conclusion about NR2E3 necessity is well-supported by the comprehensive epigenomic characterization, though causality is inferred from the genetic model rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: The introduction establishes background knowledge about rod and cone photoreceptor function, gene expression patterns, transcription factor control, and the rd7 mouse model, including that rods respond to single photons, cones mediate color vision, and rd7 rods show partial cell fate conversion.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C10 present established knowledge from the literature with appropriate citations. These are background claims that set up the study's context and are well-supported by the cited references.

results.result: Background information establishes that accessible chromatin correlates with low DNA methylation, rod nuclei are small (~5 μm) with highly condensed chromatin and inverted organization thought to facilitate nocturnal vision, while cone nuclei are larger with conventional chromatin arrangement.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C17 present established knowledge from the literature with appropriate citations. These background claims provide important context for interpreting the study's findings about the unusual relationship between methylation and accessibility in rods.

results.result: Background literature establishes concepts of vestigial enhancers, chromatin compaction during oligodendrocyte differentiation, progressive chromatin restriction during differentiation, and ONECUT1 function in cone development.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36, C49, C88, C107-C108 present established knowledge from cited literature that provides conceptual framework for interpreting the study's findings. The citations appear appropriate for the claims made.

results.result: The authors propose potential applications of their findings for understanding clinical variability in inherited retinal diseases and for refining stem cell-based therapies, suggesting regulatory sequence differences could contribute to phenotypic heterogeneity.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C120 present speculative applications of the findings. While the proposals are reasonable, they represent future directions rather than demonstrated results. The claims about clinical variability are plausible but not tested in this study.

results.result: The transgenic mouse models used for nuclear purification appeared morphologically normal with no retinal degeneration, and INTACT purification of rod photoreceptors achieved 97.5% specificity (96.7-98.2%; n=5).
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C123 provide quality control data for the experimental system. The specificity measurement is quantitative with replication (n=5) and includes confidence intervals. This validates the purity of the cell populations analyzed.

results.result: The study's main finding is that most rod-specific regions of low DNA methylation are not in accessible chromatin in adult rods, and the authors propose these are potential active regulatory sites in fetal neural tissue that remain hypo-methylated due to chromatin condensation blocking methyltransferases.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C20 present the central discovery and interpretation. C18 is well-supported by quantitative data. C19 is supported by fetal tissue comparisons. C20 is a mechanistic hypothesis supported by correlative evidence from rd7 rods but not directly tested. The overall result is a major finding but the mechanism remains somewhat speculative.
